analysis.one_liner: Extends the Military Lending Act's 36% interest rate cap and lending protections to all consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, with 15 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party, and has seen no committee action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Members of the military are already protected from some of the worst lending products: the Military Lending Act caps costs at 36% per year, bans certain fees, and lets victims cancel bad contracts. This bill extends those same protections to every American borrower. Payday loans, installment loans, and high-cost credit cards would have to live under the same cap, with mortgages and standard car-purchase loans left out. The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary borrowers who use high-cost credit: payday, installment, and title loan customers, rent-to-own buyers, and credit card holders whose rates exceed the 36% cap — disproportionately lower-income and subprime households.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Military Lending Act's consumer protections to all borrowers, the same way the law now applies them to service members and their families [S2].
The bill's core is a cap that limits the cost of consumer credit to 36% per year for all consumers, not just those in uniform [S2].
It preserves stronger state consumer protection laws and lets state attorneys general and state regulators enforce the new federal rules in court [S2].

It removes the Consumer Bureau's power to exempt particular lenders from the rule, and requires the Bureau to write implementing rules within one year, in consultation with the Department of Defense [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The consumer credit industry — payday, installment, and title lenders, rent-to-own sellers, and card issuers with subprime-rate portfolios — would lose the ability to charge rates and fees above the cap. Some high-risk borrowers could find fewer legal lenders willing to extend credit to them.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: a hard rate cap can shrink legal credit for the riskiest borrowers, who may then turn to unregulated or offshore lenders, as critics of rate caps have long argued. The bill contains no provision to replace the lost supply of small-dollar credit [S2].

The bill leaves major credit products out: residential mortgages and standard car-purchase loans secured by the car are exempt, so some of the largest and most expensive debts a household takes on are untouched [S2].

Credit card fees that comply with an existing disclosure rule are not counted toward the cap, narrowing the protection for cardholders — though credit insurance and add-on products sold with cards still count [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers currently paying triple-digit annualized rates on small-dollar loans, the benefit is direct and large: the cost of borrowing would be capped, and military families have had this protection for years without the collapse of legal credit that critics warn about. The real trade-off is that some high-risk borrowers may lose access to legal credit, and the exemptions for mortgages and car loans mean the cap doesn't reach the biggest debts. On balance the bill is a meaningful consumer gain, though a partial one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and immediately referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and with no Republican cosponsors it has no clear path forward this session.

narrative.text: Senator Reed introduced the Predatory Lending Elimination Act on February 5, 2026, with 15 Democratic colleagues joining as cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which is the last action recorded [S4].

The bill would write the Military Lending Act's protections, including a 36% annual cost cap, into the Truth in Lending Act so they apply to all consumers, with rules due from the Consumer Bureau within a year of enactment [S2].
Congress remains in session, so the bill is not dead — but with no committee action since referral and no support across the aisle, it has not moved toward a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, no one has gained from an outcome — but the consumer lending industry is better off with the bill parked in committee than it would be under a 36% cap.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its one-sentence framing speech, extending military lending protections to all borrowers.

for.name: 15 Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill a full bench on the Democratic side but none on the Republican side.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction; no action taken
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on the day of introduction and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote recorded since.

against.name: Payday and high-cost consumer lending industry
against.role: Industry opposed to national rate caps
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed national rate caps like the 36% limit proposed here, which would make its core small-dollar lending model unprofitable; its opposition to similar measures is widely reported, though it does not appear in this bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by Republicans; no Republican has joined.

industries.note: A 36% annual cost cap applies to consumer credit generally, so high-cost small-dollar lending would become unprofitable for these lenders. Their revenue comes from borrowers who pay far more than that cap allows.

Most card rates sit below 36%, so the cap binds mainly on subprime portfolios, but the bill counts fees and add-on products like credit insurance toward the cost limit, tightening how issuers price those accounts.
Rent-to-own transactions historically fall under Military Lending Act coverage, which this bill extends to all consumers, subjecting the industry to the 36% cap for the first time.
Federal credit unions are explicitly exempt from the bill's cap, so they could serve the small-dollar borrowers other lenders abandon — a competitive advantage created by the bill.
Residential mortgages and standard secured car-purchase loans are exempted, keeping the biggest household credit products outside the cap and leaving their pricing untouched.

analysis.trajectory: A bill with only Democratic cosponsors that has sat in the Republican-led Banking Committee since February 2026 is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote this session. This kind of rate cap has been proposed repeatedly without advancing; the realistic path is reintroduction in future sessions unless control of the committee changes.
